entry.title: Julia Explained: The Language Built for Speed and Science
entry.summary:
Introduction
Scientific computing has long suffered a two-language problem: prototype in Python or MATLAB, then rewrite the slow parts in C or Fortran. Julia, released in 2012, was built to end that split — a language that reads like a scripting language and runs like a compiled one. It powers climate models, drug discovery, and the world's largest telescopes, and its secret is a design choice most languages never make: multiple dispatch, where the function that runs depends on the types of all its arguments. Julia's model rests on a few distinctive ideas: Multiple dispatch — define one function name with many methods, and Julia picks the right one based on every argument's type, not just the first. entry.title: The eMudhra Certificate-Key Incident: Why Updating Windows May Not Update Your App
entry.summary: A certificate authority incident is a trust-store problem, but not every application uses the same trust store. Cloudflare reported that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised: six used for TLS and two for code signing. If a trusted certificate key is exposed, attackers may be able to create certificates or sign content that appears to chain to a trusted authority. Microsoft’s October 26 response explicitly says the issue was in eMudhra’s certificate hierarchy, not a compromise of Microsoft systems. The response has several layers. Microsoft described updates to the Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List, an Edge/WebView2 CRLSet, and an out-of-band Windows update removing seven certificates associated with the affected hierarchies. Its post said an Edge trust-list change was planned for October 27, so administrators should check the current rollout status rather than assume every device has received it. The engineering lesson is that the operating system’s browser trust store is only one part of the picture. Cloudflare notes that applications with bundled or custom trust stores need separate assessment. Its guidance also calls out dependency updates, image rebuilds, and the reloads or restarts needed to activate them. A browser test does not prove that a background service using a different TLS verifier is protected. For teams responding to this incident: Check the current guidance from your OS, browser, and application vendors. Inventory custom CA bundles and container base images. Rebuild and redeploy affected images, then restart services where required. Verify through the application’s actual TLS path. Avoid restoring trust to affected hierarchies without a documented need and risk review. Sources: Microsoft MSRC response and Cloudflare’s technical analysis. More of my work is at RaktimRanjit.com.
